name: Pedro Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Early starts. I'm doing mechanical engineering, and I live at home in a village about an hour from the university, so I'm on the 6:40 bus most mornings. My father runs a small dairy farm with my uncle, and when I'm back I help with the evening milking. On Saturdays I work at the hardware shop in town, cutting keys and mixing paint, for a wage that goes straight into the bus pass and books.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does the course feel compared with the farm?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Honestly, a bit unreal. On the farm if a pump fails, you fix it or you lose milk. In the lecture hall we draw a pump on a screen and calculate what would happen. I like that I'm learning why things work, but I miss having dirty hands, and some of the other students have never changed a tyre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's what I thought all along. People get excited over every new machine, and most of it ends up as a small help. On the farm we've got a milking system with a computer in it, and it still needs my dad in the shed at five in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be glad but not relaxed. The degree costs money I don't have, and no family savings behind me, since the farm eats whatever comes in. If milk prices drop again, everything at home gets tight, whether AI is clever or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going: lectures, Saturday at the hardware shop, evening milking. I'd ask the shop manager, Mr Hartmann, for more hours in the summer. And I'd think harder about whether a degree is the right road, or whether an apprenticeship would have been better, because I'd have been paid from the start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, in the way the weather is steady. Nothing exciting, a lot of work, and I'm used to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd think about an apprenticeship. What's pulling you that way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The wage and the hands. An apprentice gets paid to learn, but I'm paying the university to learn, and my father notices that every time the loan letter comes. I haven't told him I think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any computer tools to help with your studies?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not the AI ones. I use the library and the lecture notes. I want to know the thing myself, not ask a machine to know it for me.

say: I'd say that's what I thought all along: new machines end up a **small help**.
I'd mention the farm's milking computer still needs my **dad** at five.
think: I'm glad but not relaxed: the degree costs money I don't have, and the farm eats any **savings**.
If milk prices fall, home gets tight whatever AI does, because **milk** pays for everything.
do: Keep up lectures, the **hardware shop** and the evening milking.
Ask Mr Hartmann for more hours in the **summer**.
Think harder about an **apprenticeship** instead of the degree.
feel: **Steady**, like the weather: no excitement, a lot of work.
S0.quote: An apprentice gets paid to learn, but I'm paying the university to learn, and my father notices that every time the loan letter comes
fieldNote: His worry is the **farm's** milk price and the loan, not AI.
He quietly wonders about an **apprenticeship**, which he hasn't told his father.
He avoids AI tools because he wants to **know** the thing himself.

steps.text: Keep working Saturdays at the hardware shop
Ask Mr Hartmann for more hours in the summer
Look up local engineering apprenticeships before next term

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. It's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that sounds like a lot of change for people who sit at desks, and I'd be careful about saying more. I'd tell friends from the village that the thinking jobs are the ones to worry about, and the people who can fix things with their hands are safer for longer. I'd say it quietly at church, because older people there are afraid of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel torn. Mechanical engineering has drawing and calculation in it, and those are exactly the checking and planning tasks on the card. But the hands-on parts, like building and repairing, are further away from AI. I think I'm half exposed and half safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd focus on the practical modules, like machining and manufacturing, and look for a placement at a workshop or factory. I'd stick with my own methods for learning, but I'd have to see what the AI drawing tools do, if my tutors require them. And I'd keep the hardware shop job, because it teaches me how ordinary customers think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. I don't enjoy being told I have to change, but I'd rather change a little than be left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about back home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My father's neighbours, the older farmers who've never used a smartphone. If every supplier moves online, they'd be lost. I'd help the old farmers on our road with the online forms, because they've fed this village for forty years and nobody's showing them how.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the dairy do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle would be the one to try the new things first, because he likes gadgets. My father would say 'show me it works'. I'd probably be the bridge, which I don't love, since I don't use that stuff myself.

say: I'd say it's a lot of change for people at **desks**, and I'd speak carefully.
I'd say the people who can fix things with their **hands** are safer for longer.
think: I feel **torn**: drawing and calculation are on the card, but building and repair are further away.
do: Focus on **practical modules** like machining and look for a factory placement.
Learn what the **AI drawing tools** do only if tutors require them.
Keep the **hardware shop** job to learn how customers think.
feel: **Uneasy**: I'd rather change a little than be left behind.
S1.quote: I'd help the old farmers on our road with the online forms, because they've fed this village for forty years and nobody's showing them how
fieldNote: He judges himself **half exposed**, so his mood is anxious, not calm.
He worries about the **old farmers** on his road.
He sees himself as a reluctant **bridge** between farm and technology.

steps.text: Choose machining and manufacturing modules for second year
Apply for a placement at a local factory workshop
Help the old farmers on our road with online forms
Keep the Saturday hardware shop job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. It's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too much too quickly, and that no one asked the people it would affect. I'd tell the family that we should hold on to what's ours, which is the land and the skills. I'd say it plainly at the dinner table, and I'd say it again at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be scared. I've just started, and the thinking part of my degree would be done by AI before I finish. I'd have a loan and a certificate for a job that's gone. My father can't help, and my uncle would say we should sell up if things get hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my father about whether I should leave university and look for an apprenticeship in a trade like machining or electrics, where the robots take three more years to arrive. I'd throw myself into helping the farm, because food will always be needed. And I'd go to the church group and ask who is hiring or knows a master tradesman who needs an apprentice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Like a stone in my stomach. I'd try to hide it from my mother, but she'd notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your father?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd like to work with him and my uncle on the farm while I work out what's next. I'd tell my father that I won't let the farm fall because I was too proud to leave the degree. He'd say nothing, but he'd understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would the three-year delay matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives hands-on trades some breathing room, but I wouldn't count on it. Robots in a milking shed may be slower than software, but they're still coming. It buys time, not safety.

say: I'd say it's **too much, too quickly**, and no one asked those affected.
I'd tell the family to hold on to what's **ours**: land and skills.
think: I'd be **scared**: the thinking part of my degree would be done by AI before I finish.
I'd have a **loan** and a certificate for a job that's gone.
do: Talk to my father about leaving for a trade **apprenticeship** in machining or electrics.
Throw myself into **farm** work, since food will always be needed.
Ask the church group who knows a **master tradesman**.
feel: **Heavy**, like a stone in my stomach, hidden from my mother.
S2.quote: I'd tell my father that I won't let the farm fall because I was too proud to leave the degree
fieldNote: He is ready to **leave** the degree, which shows how sharply he feels the risk.
He leans on **family and church** for work leads.
He treats the three-year gap as time bought, not **safety**.

steps.text: Ask my father whether I should leave university
Look for a machining or electrics apprenticeship
Ask the church group for a master tradesman who needs help
Work more evenings and weekends on the farm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fourth picture. It's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is not enough to feel safe, but enough to act. I'd tell my friends from the village that they should learn a trade or a skill that's useful anywhere. I'd say that families need to stick together and look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel slightly better than with two years. I'd finish the degree and have a couple of years of work before it lands. But I'd be 23, carrying a loan, and I'd have chosen a path that's uncertain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree but with a plan to get hands-on work, probably in manufacturing or repair, where robots are slower. I'd spend summers at the farm and hardware shop, because they keep me connected. I'd also save for the loan and talk to my father about whether we can modernise the dairy, with me helping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried but not frozen. I've got time to do something, and that's how I like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would modernising the dairy look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A better milking system with sensors, which saves time and shows when a cow is sick. If I come home with an engineering degree, our dairy should be the one on the road that's run by someone who understands the machines. My father would be sceptical, but it would show him the degree has a use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be different with only two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave the degree and learn a trade at once. Five years means I can finish and bring something back, and that's the difference.

say: I'd say five years is **not enough** to feel safe, but enough to act.
I'd say families need to **stick together** and look after each other.
think: I'd feel better than with two years: I'd finish and have a few years of **work**.
I'd be 23 with a **loan** on an uncertain path.
do: Finish the degree but aim for **hands-on** work in manufacturing or repair.
Spend summers at the **farm** and the hardware shop.
Talk to my father about **modernising** the dairy.
feel: **Worried** but not frozen, with time to act.
S3.quote: If I come home with an engineering degree, our dairy should be the one on the road that's run by someone who understands the machines
fieldNote: He sees his degree as something to **bring home** to the dairy.
Five years lets him **finish**, whereas two would push him into a trade.
He keeps strong **family** ties in his plan.

steps.text: Choose a manufacturing project and a repair-focused placement
Draw up a plan to add sensors to the dairy's milking system
Talk to my father about me working on the farm after graduating
Save towards the loan from summer wages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fifth and last picture. It's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is long enough to prepare, but only if people stop ignoring it. I'd tell my friends from the village to look at apprenticeships and trades, because those hold up longer. I'd say that the family and the community will carry people through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel fine about myself. By 28 I'd have the degree, work behind me, and probably a family. The worry is that the farm may not survive, and that my children would grow up in a world where nobody needs what I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, work in industry for a few years, and put money into the farm. I'd learn the new tools when they've proven to be useful, because I don't trust fads. And I'd marry, I hope, and start a family while there's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. It's like knowing winter is coming and having a full woodshed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the full woodshed look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Savings, skills, and a family. I'd rather have a woodshed than an app, meaning a small plot of land, a trade in my hands and a house that's paid off. Those hold up whatever happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if it arrived sooner than ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd already be ahead of most people, with skills and savings. I'd be unhappy, but not helpless.

say: I'd say ten years is **long enough**, but only if people stop ignoring it.
I'd tell friends to look at **apprenticeships** and trades.
think: I'd feel fine about myself, but worry the **farm** may not survive.
I'd worry my future **children** would grow up where nobody needs what I know.
do: Finish the degree, work in **industry** and put money into the farm.
Learn the new **tools** only once they've proven useful.
feel: Fairly **calm**, like knowing winter is coming with a full woodshed.
S4.quote: I'd rather have a woodshed than an app, meaning a small plot of land, a trade in my hands and a house that's paid off
fieldNote: He thinks in terms of **land, trade and family**, which is a traditional outlook.
He trusts a tool only once it has proven itself, which fits his **resistant** side.
The **farm's** survival is his main worry even with ten years.

steps.text: Work in industry for a few years and pay down the loan
Put part of my wages into the family dairy
Marry and start a family once the loan is under control

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because it asks me to decide between the degree and a trade with the farm in trouble and no savings. What would help is apprenticeships that pay, and some honesty from the university about whether the course will still be worth it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not scared of change, I'm scared of being told to change without being shown. I'd rather learn a trade slowly with an old master than be told by a screen that I'm already behind.

headlineQuote: I'd rather learn a trade slowly with an old master than be told by a screen that I'm already behind
portrait: Pedro is an **18-year-old** mechanical engineering first-year from a dairy farm, working Saturdays at a hardware shop.
He is traditional and resistant, valuing work, faith, family and apprenticeships over debt and handouts.
He has never used AI tools and wants to know things himself rather than ask a machine.
His worries are the farm's milk price, the loan and neighbours who'd be lost online.
His mood runs from uneasy to alarmed at two years, when he'd consider leaving for a trade.
biggestWorry: The **2028** scenario worries him most, since it forces a choice between degree and trade.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **paid** apprenticeships and honest word from the university about the course's worth.
